content: Mithridate, also referred to as mithridatum, mithridatium, or mithridaticum, is a semi-mythical antidote reputed to contain as many as 65 ingredients. It was originally formulated as a remedy for poisoning and is attributed to Mithridates VI of Pontus. This complex preparation was one of the most sought-after medicinal compounds during the Renaissance, particularly in Italy and France, where it remained in use for centuries. An updated version of the recipe, known as theriac (Theriacum Andromachi), continued to be recognized well into the 19th century. The name mithridate derives from its creator, Mithridates VI, the King of Pontus, who is said to have fortified his body against poisons by regularly consuming antidotes and preservatives. According to legend, his immunity to poisons was so complete that he was unable to end his own life using poison. The recipe for mithridate was reportedly discovered in his personal cabinet, written in his own hand, and later brought to Rome by Pompey. It was subsequently translated into verse by Servilius Damocrates, a renowned physician, and later by Galen. Over time, the formula likely underwent significant modifications from its original version. Mithridate was also employed as part of a regimen to protect against the plague. Simon Kellwaye, writing in 1593, recommended a preparation involving a large onion hollowed out and filled with mithridate or treacle, along with some rue leaves. Physicians in London were still officially prescribing mithridate as late as 1786. Over time, the term mithridate came to refer to any general-purpose antidote. Aulus Cornelius Celsus, in his work De Medicina (circa 30 AD), provided one of the earliest detailed formulations of mithridate. His recipe included a wide array of ingredients, such as costmary, sweet flag, hypericum, gum, sagapenum, acacia juice, Illyrian iris, cardamom, anise, Gallic nard, gentian root, dried rose leaves, poppy tears, parsley, cassia, saxifrage, darnel, long pepper, storax, castoreum, frankincense, hypocistis juice, myrrh, opopanax, malabathrum leaves, turpentine resin, galbanum, Cretan carrot seeds, nard, opobalsam, shepherd's purse, rhubarb root, saffron, ginger, and cinnamon. These ingredients were ground into a powder and mixed with honey. For poisoning, a dose the size of an almond was administered in wine, while for other ailments, a dose the size of an Egyptian bean was deemed sufficient. Notably, some ingredients, such as Illyrian iris, darnel, and rhubarb, were unique to Celsus' version of the antidote. Galen later referred to the antidote as theriac and documented various versions of the formula, including those by Aelius (used by Julius Caesar), Andromachus (physician to Nero), Antipater, Nicostratus, and Damocrates. The formulation by Andromachus closely resembled that of Celsus. The production of antidotes labeled as mithridate or theriac (the English term treacle is derived from this) persisted into the 19th century. Ephraim Chambers, in his 1728 Cyclopaedia, described mithridate as a principal medicine in apothecaries' shops, composed of numerous ingredients such as opium, myrrh, agaric, saffron, ginger, cinnamon, spikenard, frankincense, castor, pepper, gentian, and others. It was regarded as a cordial, opiate, sudorific, and alexipharmic. Petrus Andreas Matthiolus considered mithridate to be more effective against poisons than Venice treacle and easier to prepare. However, skepticism about mithridate and similar theriacs, with their extensive lists of ingredients, was expressed as early as the 1st century AD by Pliny the Elder.
